newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. Senator Cohen, in Taiwan, coy on Pentagon post.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senator Cohen, in Taiwan, coy on Pentagon post.

text.p: Retiring U.S. Senator William Cohen, widely tipped to become the next U.S. secretary of defence, slipped in a subtle pitch for the post on Tuesday during a visit to the Pacific strategic flashpoint of Taiwan.

With fellow Senator Sam Nunn jokingly calling him "Secretary Cohen", the Maine Republican said he hoped President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, would adopt a bipartisan policy when filling cabinet vacancies for his second term.

"I know the president has expressed a desire to have a bipartisan defence policy...and I think it is in the interest of the country that we establish such a policy," Cohen told reporters at the close of a three-day Taipei visit.
Cohen, giving up his Senate seat at year's end, would not say if he had discussed the post with Clinton despite reports that he dropped by the White House last week.
"So far it's only a matter of speculation and it has not moved beyond that," Cohen said of his chances.
Nunn, himself touted to have an outside shot to run the Pentagon or State Department, said he planned to leave government service after departing the Senate in December.
But the Georgia Democrat, a military and strategic affairs expert, declined to say if he would accept or decline an offer.
"Secretary Cohen and I haven't discussed that," Nunn quipped as Cohen smiled.
"It's always an honour to be mentioned for any cabinet position, particularly a high-level position, but my plans now are to return to the private sector," Nunn said.
Defence Secretary William Perry and Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who is visiting Beijing this week, have told Clinton they will not stay on for a second term.
Cohen and Nunn are among nine U.S. senators who in November have visited Taiwan -- which was rattled by China's war games and missile tests in the weeks prior to its presidential election in March.
Beijing's manoeuvres prompted Clinton to dispatch two aircraft carrier groups to the area -- the biggest U.S. naval presence near the island since the Vietnam War.
A U.S. Navy study concluded the war games were practice for a potential invasion of the Nationalist-ruled island which China has regarded as a rebel province since a civil war in 1949.

Nunn, who in 1994 was replaced as chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee after the Republicans took control of the Senate, echoed Washington's long-standing policy of reserving a right to arm and defend Taiwan if necessary.

"We want to be sure that we do everything we can in our military deployments, our overall alliances and our friendship as well as our arms sales to promote peace and stability" between Taiwan and China, Nunn said.
Beijing vows to attack if Taiwan seeks independence.
Washington switched recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979, but Clinton policy has been that improvement of U.S. ties with China should not be at Taiwan's expense.
Cohen echoed that policy in Taipei where he and Nunn met President Lee Teng-hui and other leaders.

"I don't think the Clinton administration or any administration has in mind a zero-sum game -- that if we have better relations with mainland China, it means we have a reduction in support for Taiwan," Cohen said.
